extracted.intended_audience: military officers, judge advocates, and other military legal personnel
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal standards and administrative rules governing military confinement, prison administration, use of force, corporal punishment, procedural limits of investigatory boards/courts, and related matters (also includes discussion of the eight-hour law as applied to public works and contractors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commencement of confinement
rubrics_metrics.description: "the confinement shall be considered as commencing at the date of the promulgation of the sentence in orders."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under General Order 21 (Headquarters of the Army, 1870) confinement begins at date sentence is promulgated in orders; commencement is not to be delayed until notice reaches the prisoner so as to avoid abuses the order intended to correct. (Citations: R.30,150, Mar. 1870; G.18165, Dec. 26, 1905; Jan. 12, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative sentences and commencement of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soldier at two successive trials is sentenced to confinement the two sentences will be held to be cumulative when they are both approved on the same day or when the soldier is serving one sentence when brought to trial a second time resulting in confinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a sentence is cumulative upon a pending sentence, execution of the later sentence properly commences at the date when the pending confinement term terminates (whether by expiration or remission). Principle applies even where prisoner escaped, enlisted, deserted, was arrested, tried and sentenced. (Multiple citations: R.34,469 Sept.1873; C.1608 Aug.1,1895; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to serve unexecuted portion after escape
rubrics_metrics.description: When a military prisoner escapes, he must upon capture serve the unexecuted portion of his sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when escape occurs as an accused during trial and later sentenced to confinement which is approved and ordered executed; also when prisoner escapes after sentence but before approval by reviewing authority; and when escaping pending execution of sentence. One hundred and third article of war does not prevent requirement to serve remainder upon capture. (Citations: G.14767 Feb.6, 1905; 23941 Oct.7,1908; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prisoners' mail privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Prison authorities have no right to open and inspect letters addressed to or sent by their prisoners without the consent of the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities may retain such letters unopened until parties are tried or released, or dispose of them under judicial process, but cannot open/inspect without consent. (Citation: C.2469 July, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of court-martial sentence is without precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The suspension of the sentence of a court martial before or during its execution is without precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A post commander is not authorized under the one hundred and twelfth article of war to suspend execution of a sentence by a garrison court-martial during good behavior of soldiers so sentenced. (Citations: C.8838 Aug.1900; R.30,115 Feb.1870; C.20797 Dec.13,1906; 27738 Jan.21,1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of remission on sentence and good-conduct time
rubrics_metrics.description: A remission of part of a sentence of confinement leaves the reduced sentence as though it were the original, and the prisoner is entitled to good-conduct time on the reduced sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remission does not change entitlement to good-conduct credit; references: R.37,490 Apr.1876; P.44,66 Nov.1890.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeds from prisoner-manufactured articles are public funds
rubrics_metrics.description: The proceeds of sales of articles manufactured by the prisoners at the military prison are public funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of statutory provision regarding disposition (section 1351, R.S. only requires they be 'accounted for'), such proceeds cannot legally be expended in repairing or improving the prison building or otherwise without authority of Congress. (Citation: R.42,24 Oct.1878.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War authority over disposition of convict-made goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the general authority vested in the Secretary of War by section 1351, R.S., the Secretary may direct disposition of articles manufactured by convicts (e.g., order shoes be turned over to Quartermaster Department for issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no statute precludes such action, the Secretary's general authority permits ordering convict-made goods to be transferred for Army use. (Citation: R.41,427 Oct.1878.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prison labor not additional punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a prisoner to perform work prescribed for prisoners of his class by statute is not adding to the punishment even if 'hard labor' is not in terms included in the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons sentenced to imprisonment at military prison may be legally employed in labor or at trades indicated by section 1351, R.S., even where 'hard labor' is not explicitly in the sentence. (Citations: R.37,640 June,1876; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prison commander authority and limited use of force
rubrics_metrics.description: Commander of a prison post is authorized to make and enforce necessary and proper regulations for safe keeping and government of military prisoners and may use force, if needful, but no more force than necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commander may prevent civilians from landing in violation of regulations and put them off the island; in extreme cases (e.g., civilian aiding prisoner escape and no other means avail), he may properly order firing upon the party. Use of force must be necessary and proportionate. (Citation: R.32,525 Apr.1872.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Private money of prisoner not forfeitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Private money of a general prisoner confined in a United States military prison may not be forfeited even if received as a bribe for assisting in violating prison rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If taken possession of by the commandant it must be returned to the general prisoner at date of release. (Citations: C.26782 May 28, 1910; 25281 Aug.17,1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure after guard kills prisoner to prevent escape
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a member of a military prison guard shot and killed a general prisoner to prevent escape, it is not good policy to issue a pardon to restore him to duty without trial even though innocent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a soldier should be kept in military hands and arraigned before a general court-martial to determine justification for extreme measures. (C.27119 Aug.3,1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible prison industries (example: tailor shop)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tailor shop can be established in the military prison at which general prisoners can be employed in the making of civilian clothing for issue to discharged general prisoners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishment and employment in such shops is authorized by cited opinions. (C.26193 Feb.10 & Mar.12, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery to penitentiary by military authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons convicted by courts-martial and sent to the United States penitentiary under the civil act of March 2, 1895, cannot be turned over to a United States marshal for transportation to the penitentiary but must be delivered there by the military authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military authorities are required to deliver such convicts; (C.1201 July,1895; 20052 July 13, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective duty of the guard to prevent escapes
rubrics_metrics.description: The guard at a military post must be considered as a whole; assignment of certain members to watch certain designated prisoners does not relieve other members of the guard of the duty of preventing the escape of prisoners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual assignments do not absolve collective responsibility; example cited where sentinel fired and killed an escaping prisoner (C.23423 June 12, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegality of arbitrary punitive treatment by officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Punitive treatment by officers (tying up, gagging, immersion, striking with a rifle causing severe injury, etc.) without legal sanction is wholly without justification and constitutes a military offense by the officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers who inflict such punishments are amenable to trial (e.g., under article 62); cases recommend bringing officers to trial and advising clemency for soldiers subjected to such treatment. (Citations: P.60,257 June,1893; P.43,62 June,1893; R.53,193 Oct.,1886.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for sentinels enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect for the person and office of a sentinel is strictly enjoined by military law; all persons of whatever rank are required to observe respect toward sentinels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentinels have grave responsibility; molesting or interfering with them without penalty would be prejudicial to service; an officer who assaulted a sentinel could be dismissed. (B.18,698 Feb.,1866.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Company commander lacks authority to buy off trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A company commander has no authority to require a soldier to contribute money to the company fund in lieu of trial by court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct is unauthorized and unlawful. (C.20061 July 13, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on pay stoppage under 54th article
rubrics_metrics.description: The pay of the offender or offenders can be resorted to under the fifty-fourth article of war only for the purpose of the 'reparation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A military commander may not add further stoppage by way of punishment beyond reparation. (R.8,671 July,1864.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on reviewing officer's power after disapproving acquittal
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing officer is not authorized, after disapproving an acquittal, to order that the accused be confined or otherwise punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewing authority cannot substitute confinement or punishment after disapproving an acquittal. (R.12,249 Jan.,1865.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to ranks statutory limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to the ranks was authorized as a punishment for certain offenses by acts during the Civil War but such punishment is no longer legal; statutory provisions are confined to the Civil War period and not reenacted in the Revised Statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic statutory authorizations existed (acts of March 3, 1863; March 12, 1863) but have been judicially limited to that period. (C.22215 Oct.15,1907; citation to R.16, JAS, Aug.1865 for context.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigatory boards lack judicial powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A board of officers convened to investigate (obtain or hear and examine evidence) and report cannot, in absence of specific statutory authority, exercise any of the peculiar legal functions either of a court-martial or of a court of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a board cannot swear witnesses, cannot compel civilian witnesses to appear, cannot try nor sentence, has no 'accused' party entitled to appear as before a court-martial, is not restricted by statute of limitations, and may present multiple reports where members cannot concur. (Citations: R.2, SIfi May,1863; 21,835 Apr.,1866; 26,492 Mar.,1868; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of inquiry not available for civilians; board of investigation limited
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of inquiry cannot be ordered in a case of a civilian; a body of officers convened to inquire into facts of a dismissed officer's case is a mere board of investigation and can exercise none of the special powers of a court-martial or court of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board is limited to fact-finding and reporting; does not have inquiry/court powers over civilians. (R.41,263 June,1878.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No witness fees for preliminary-only testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties who appeared and testified before, and at the instance of, an officer charged with the preliminary investigation of a case, but were not required to attend at the subsequent trial, were not legally entitled to witness fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary investigatory attendance does not entitle witnesses to fees unless attendance at trial is required. (R.21,463 July,1866.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriations for courts and reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Army appropriation acts appropriate money 'for expenses of courts-martial, courts of inquiry, and compensation of reporters and witnesses attending the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters for courts of inquiry may be paid from such appropriations; employment of a reporter for a board of officers must be authorized by the Secretary of War and payment would come from contingent Army expenses. (a.6971 Sept.,1899.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eight-hour law: scope and 'public works' not narrowly construed
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of August 1, 1892 (eight-hour law) is to be given a broad construction; the term 'public works of the United States' should not be narrowly construed and covers works of river and harbor improvement and similar works even where the United States does not own the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original 1868 statute was a direction and not a contract; the 1892 act cured that defect. Examples include construction of levees per Mississippi River Commission plans; public works include river/harbor works, railways, canals, waterworks, roads, and probably public buildings though no decision expressly includes buildings. (Citations: U.S. v. Martin 94 U.S.; P.55,155 Aug.22,1892; C.18811 Nov.4,1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eight-hour law: contractors' obligations and self-acting nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not essential that the requirements of the eight-hour act be embodied in a contract; the law is self-acting and contractors are directly responsible to comply irrespective of contract terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers who enter contracts are not charged with enforcing the law vis-a-vis contractors; any departmental construction that is erroneous will not protect contractors from prosecution. (P.55,311 Sept.7,1892; C.11459 Nov.4,1901; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eight-hour law: vessels and repairs exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Repairs made to a Government vessel at a private contractor's plant (where the vessel is out of active Government control) are generally not regarded as work on a 'public work' for purposes of the eight-hour law; similar inapplicability to Navy vessels under construction at private establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the repairs occur at a Government dock or under conditions that keep the vessel in active Government control, the law may perhaps apply; otherwise not. (C.20169 Apr.26,1910; G.20169 Feb.27,1907; Feb.9,1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eight-hour law: classification of dredging/tug/scow workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether men employed on dredges, scows, and tugs are within the act depends on status: while ordinarily seamen (not within the act), when actually engaged in 'labor upon public work' they may come within the application; later decisions (Ellis v. U.S.) held dredging and rock-excavation workers on river and harbor improvements are not 'laborers and mechanics' within the act but are seamen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of application is for courts on trial of persons charged with violations; departmental pronouncements do not bind courts. (P.57,36 Dec.13,1892; C.20169 Mar.16 & 21,1907; Ellis v. U.S. 206 U.S. 246.)
